subject: convert intercepts to difficulties in bifactor model

messages.author: 9e35739f18a45ee9
messages.subject: convert intercepts to difficulties in bifactor model
parts:
Hi, I've calculated a bifactor model using bfactor(), and would like to convert the intercept terms for the general factor to conventional IRT difficulties.  Is this possible?

Thanks!

Tyler

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: convert intercepts to difficulties in bifactor model
parts:
On Thu, Dec 15, 2016 at 2:28 PM, Tyler Moore <reduct...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi, I've calculated a bifactor model using bfactor(), and would like to convert the intercept terms for the general factor to conventional IRT difficulties.  Is this possible?

What is a 'conventional' difficulty parameter in a multidimensional model? The difficulty parameter (often called b) represents the point of inflection along the response function in a one-dimensional model; for a 2PL model, this occurs when the expected probability = 0.5, for example. 

With multiple dimensions, a single value to represent the inflection point is not possible because it's really an infinite vector of locations where the inflection occurs (hence, it requires a function of inputs to compute). So I don't really think you want this type of parameter in a multidimensional model. Cheers.   
 

Thanks!

Tyler

messages.author: 9e35739f18a45ee9
messages.subject: Re: convert intercepts to difficulties in bifactor model
parts:
Hi Phil, thanks very much for the quick response.  I take your point, but I figured since factors in a bifactor model are almost always orthogonal (as they are in my case), it would be possible to estimate conventional difficulties for each factor's items as they relate to their own thetas independent of the other thetas.  It would seem like a straightforward problem, but the message boards (this one, IRTPRO, etc.) get this question a lot with no clear answers (as far as I can see).  I did find this explanation from the Vector group (probably written by Li Cai, but I'm not sure):

[He/She first gives the caveat that this provides only an approximation.]  First, put the slopes on the approximate Normal metric by dividing each by the IRT scaling constant 1.7. Then compute the sum of squares of the rescaled slopes. Add 1.0 to the result and take its square root; this gives you the constant you will need to convert all the intercepts.  To convert the intercepts, first add a minus sign and then divide the intercepts by 1.7 to also make them on the normal metric. Then divide each intercept by the constant found above. You use the same constant for all the intercepts in this item. When you move on to the next item, however, you will need to repeat the process for finding the conversion constant.  For example, if an item was found to have slope parameters of a1 = 1.28 and a2 = 1.67, the conversion constant would be found by sqrt((1.28/1.7)2+(1.67/1.7)2+1) = 1.59.  If the first intercept value was 5.35, the converted threshold parameter may be obtained from first putting the intercept on the Normal metric (-5.35/1.7 = -3.15) and then dividing by the conversion constant (-3.15/ 1.59 ≈ -1.98).


The reason I'm asking is that I'm building CATs, and some CAT-building software accepts only the conventional parameters.  I need a bifactor to account for the multidimensionality (as you know; see attached), so am hoping to just use the general factor to get the best estimates possible.  Do you see anything problematic about the above suggestion, beyond that it is only an approximation?


Thanks again for the quick response - your mirt package is fantastic.

On Fri, Dec 16, 2016 at 11:54 AM, Tyler Moore <reduct...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Phil, thanks very much for the quick response.  I take your point, but I figured since factors in a bifactor model are almost always orthogonal (as they are in my case), it would be possible to estimate conventional difficulties for each factor's items as they relate to their own thetas independent of the other thetas.

But they aren't though, orthogonality isn't the main problem. It's the fact that the bifactor model is compensatory in nature that's the issue (i.e., increasing the latent trait on either the general or specific factor will necessarily increase the probability of positive responses).

It would seem like a straightforward problem, but the message boards (this one, IRTPRO, etc.) get this question a lot with no clear answers (as far as I can see).  I did find this explanation from the Vector group (probably written by Li Cai, but I'm not sure):

[He/She first gives the caveat that this provides only an approximation.]  First, put the slopes on the approximate Normal metric by dividing each by the IRT scaling constant 1.7. Then compute the sum of squares of the rescaled slopes. Add 1.0 to the result and take its square root; this gives you the constant you will need to convert all the intercepts.  To convert the intercepts, first add a minus sign and then divide the intercepts by 1.7 to also make them on the normal metric. Then divide each intercept by the constant found above. You use the same constant for all the intercepts in this item. When you move on to the next item, however, you will need to repeat the process for finding the conversion constant.  For example, if an item was found to have slope parameters of a1 = 1.28 and a2 = 1.67, the conversion constant would be found by sqrt((1.28/1.7)2+(1.67/1.7)2+1) = 1.59.  If the first intercept value was 5.35, the converted threshold parameter may be obtained from first putting the intercept on the Normal metric (-5.35/1.7 = -3.15) and then dividing by the conversion constant (-3.15/ 1.59 ≈ -1.98).


The reason I'm asking is that I'm building CATs, and some CAT-building software accepts only the conventional parameters.  I need a bifactor to account for the multidimensionality (as you know; see attached), so am hoping to just use the general factor to get the best estimates possible.  Do you see anything problematic about the above suggestion, beyond that it is only an approximation?

It's suboptimal in many senses, and throws away a good amount of useful information. Ultimately in defeats the purpose of fitting a multidimensional model as well, because approximating unidimenisonality is bound to witness some peculiar paradoxes. 

Moreover, there is software available specifically for bifactor models, and will accomplish what you are after without throwing away the model structure (e.g., see the mirtCAT package and the associated JSS paper). All you would need is to use a weighted selection criteria like W-rule, where the weight of the general factor is set to 1 and 0 for the specific factors. Then all the dependence would be accounted for, and the approximation is not required at all.

Thanks again for the quick response - your mirt package is fantastic.

Hi Phil --

I have a related question. I am interested in visualizing the items in the space of the latent traits for a 2-dimensional graded response model--essentially, a bivariate scatterplot. What I'm looking is for the vector of points (a1,a2) where either the probability for category X is at its peak or where the cutoff occurs (I'm fine with either).

What I've thought about doing is the following transformation to generalize the 1-dimensional transform:

aT*theta + d = 0
aT*theta = -d
(aT)aT*theta = -d*aT
norm(a) * theta = -d*aT
theta = -d*aT / norm(a)

T stands for the transpose operator. I believe that the right-hand side will give me the cutpoint values in two dimensions, but I wanted to check first and see if my math made any sense.
